pages.text: After a morning shower, raindrops sit like glass beads on a broad cocoyam leaf. Bend close to one and look through it. The thin veins of the leaf beneath the drop appear larger and clearer than the veins beside it. The drop is working as a magnifying glass. No one shaped or polished it, yet it bends light just as the lenses in spectacles, cameras, and microscopes do. To understand how, we need to follow what light does when it meets water. Along the way we shall measure the distance to the Moon and the depth of the sea.

pages.text: Light travels in straight lines called rays. That is why shadows have sharp edges. When rays hit a smooth, shiny surface, such as a mirror or calm water, they bounce off. This is reflection. When rays pass from one clear material into another, such as from air into water, something else happens. Light travels more slowly in water than in air, and the change of speed makes the ray change direction. This bending is called refraction. It explains why a straight stick standing in a bucket of water looks broken at the surface, and why a stream looks shallower than it really is.

pages.text: A raindrop has a curved surface. Rays passing through different parts of the curve are bent by different amounts, and all are bent inwards, towards one another. Any clear object that is thicker in the middle than at the edges does this. It is called a convex lens. The point where the rays meet is the focus. Hold a convex lens close to a small object and the object looks bigger. Your own eye contains a convex lens. It bends the light entering the eye so that a sharp picture forms on the retina, the sensitive layer at the back.

pages.text: In some eyes, the picture forms a little in front of the retina or behind it, and the world looks blurred. Spectacles add an extra lens that bends the rays just enough to correct the fault. Lenses also extend our sight. A microscope uses them to show the malaria parasite inside a drop of blood. A telescope uses them to show the moons of Jupiter. One warning: a convex lens can bring sunlight to a focus hot enough to burn paper. Never look at the Sun through a lens, and never leave one lying in dry grass.

pages.text: How fast is light? In empty space it covers about 300,000 kilometres every second, fast enough to circle Earth more than seven times in one second. Scientists use this speed as a measuring tape. Astronauts who landed on the Moon between 1969 and 1972 left special reflectors on its surface. Today, observatories fire short pulses of laser light at them and time the return. The round trip takes about 2.56 seconds. Half of that time, multiplied by the speed of light, gives the distance: about 384,000 kilometres. The measurements are so exact that they show the Moon moving away by nearly 4 centimetres a year.

pages.alt: A thin green laser beam rising from an observatory dome towards a full Moon.

pages.text: The same trick works with sound in places where light cannot go. Sea water soon swallows light, but sound travels through it well, at about 1,500 metres per second. A ship sends a pulse of sound downwards and times the echo from the sea bed. If the echo returns after 2 seconds, the sound took 1 second to go down, so the water is 1,500 metres deep. Fishing boats use echo sounders to find shoals of fish, and survey ships use them to map the sea floor off Ghana’s coast. Send a pulse, time its return, and you can measure what you cannot reach.

Thinner in the middle than at the edges

activities.question: A laser pulse takes about 2.56 seconds to reach the Moon and come back. Why do scientists use half of this time to find the distance?
options: Light slows down on the way back
The pulse travels the distance twice: there and back

activities.prompt: Put the steps of measuring the distance to the Moon in order.
items: An observatory fires a pulse of laser light
The pulse crosses space to the Moon
A reflector on the Moon sends the pulse back
The observatory records the time for the round trip
Half the time is multiplied by the speed of light
